paragraphs: Postsecondary political science teaching suits people willing to keep studying political institutions, theory, and international relations material and to turn controversies into teachable, assessable content. The work is not only lecturing; it also includes preparing classes, grading, and answering questions, and teaching-and-research positions add research and departmental service. First verify the target institution's discipline, degree, qualification, and appointment requirements.

Observable signals: willingness to trace original sources and opposing arguments; ability to assess different views by the same standard; ability to chair discussions of disagreement while respecting students; and willingness to write specific feedback on each paper. If you only like stating positions and are unwilling to verify sources or mark assignments, run a short-course trial first.

Safe work sample: using the fully fictional A1–A3 material on this page, write within 60 minutes the objectives of one comparative politics lesson, a 45-minute flow, two discussion questions, a four-dimension scoring rubric, and feedback on a fictional student passage; real students or unauthorized material must not be used.

When self-checking, look at three things: whether the 45-minute segments add up correctly; whether you recognize that a national vote share cannot be inferred from “winning 6 districts”; and whether you can point out the student's inferential error and give actionable advice. Record your own difficulties in retrieval, explanation, and grading, then ask a peer to review.

If you are willing to keep reading, explain complex institutions, guide different views into evidence-based discussion, and assess each student's learning, it is worth trying a fictional course sample. If you lean more toward independent research, compare political scientist positions; if you lean more toward school-level teaching, verify teacher qualifications and the student group separately.

Postsecondary political science teachers organize political science, international affairs, or international relations knowledge into university courses and take on lecturing, discussion, assignment assessment, and student guidance; some positions also include research. O*NET 25-1065 is the US occupational scope anchor, and the specific appointment, qualifications, and responsibility are decided by the institution and jurisdiction.
O*NET 25-1065.00: Political Science Teachers, Postsecondary; includes university teachers who are teaching-focused as well as those combining teaching and research.

Assessment and feedback｜grade papers, assignments, and examinations｜give specific feedback based on the previously announced grading criteria and keep grades and the necessary teaching records.

Research and supervision｜follow the literature, conduct research, and supervise student projects｜research-oriented positions may require papers, projects, and academic exchange; the specific proportion depends on the appointment track.

items.title: Hiring verification points and preparation suggestions

values: Materials and setup｜all are editorially designed fictional exercises

The fictional university “Qinghe College” plans one 45-minute session of its Introduction to Comparative Politics course on the theme “how different electoral systems affect representation”; no real students, schools, or election data are used.

A1 course objective: students can distinguish the seat allocation mechanisms of proportional representation and single-member district systems and can point out the evidence and limitations of at least one fairness claim.

A2 fictional rule: in place A, four groups receive 40%, 30%, 20%, and 10% of the vote, and 10 seats are allocated directly in proportion to each group's votes with no threshold; each proportion multiplied by 10 is a whole number. Place B has 10 single-member districts with one seat each, and it is only known that a certain group won 6 districts, with no district vote counts or turnout given. The two place samples do not correspond.
Tasks and outputs

Write a 45-minute teaching flow: 5 minutes of introduction, 15 minutes of mechanism comparison, 15 minutes of small-group discussion, and 10 minutes of formative assessment. Note the student output and the teacher's verification point for each segment.

A3 fictional student passage: “The first group in place A received 40% of the vote, so under any system it must necessarily get 4 seats; place B won 6 districts, so that group must have received 60% of the national vote. Proportional representation is always the fairest.” Then write two discussion questions, a four-item rubric with 0–2 points each, the item-by-item scoring basis for A3, and about 120-character feedback.
Reference delivery (answer independently before checking)

Flow example: 5 minutes to list the systems and data gaps; 15 minutes to compute 4, 3, 2, and 1 seats for place A and to clarify that place B can only be said to have 6 seats; 15 minutes to discuss “can 6 seats imply 60% of the vote” and “is fairness measured by vote-seat congruence, local representation, or another standard”; 10 minutes to use the A3 exit ticket to check mechanisms and inferences. Each segment submits a concept card, a calculation table, discussion reasons, and a correction slip respectively.

Rubric example (0–2 points each): mechanism calculation — 2 points for correct rules and calculation, 1 point for only the correct result, 0 points for an error; inference boundary — 2 points for identifying both errors: generalizing the 4 seats across systems and inferring vote share from the 6 districts, 1 point for identifying only one error, 0 points for identifying neither; fairness argument — 2 points for defining the standard and explaining its limits, 1 point for defining only, 0 points for absolutism; evidence expression — 2 points for distinguishing what A2 makes knowable from the unknown and suggesting the needed material, 1 point for partial distinction, 0 points for treating the unknown as fact. A3 can be scored 1, 0, 0, 0, for 1/8 in total, because it gives only the place A result yet draws three unsupported conclusions; the simulated scoring is not a real grade.

Feedback example: you correctly computed the 4 seats in the proportional allocation given for place A, but it holds only under the A2 rules and cannot be generalized to any system. For place B it is only known that the group won 6 districts and took 6 seats; without district vote counts and turnout, the national vote share cannot be computed. Please list what is knowable and what is unknown separately, discuss fairness using a clear standard such as vote-seat congruence or local representation, and note that comparing the two places cannot prove a causal effect of the systems.
Boundaries and review

Use fictional material only. Review that 5+15+15+10=45 minutes, that place A's 4+3+2+1=10 seats, that place B has 6 seats with the national vote unknown, and that the four 0–2 point rubric items and the total are consistent; the third item “always the fairest” must also require a standard and its limits, and it is not enough to correct only the two numerical inferences.

entries.answer: Daily work revolves around university courses: setting teaching objectives and a syllabus, choosing material on political theory, comparative politics, and international relations, lecturing and chairing discussion, designing assignments and examinations, and grading, giving feedback, and tutoring students by rubric. Teaching-and-research positions also require research, publication, and departmental service; the specific time allocation is decided by the appointment contract.
entries.question: What do postsecondary political science teachers do every day?

entries.answer: Political scientists mainly pose and study political phenomena, policy, or institutional questions and may work in research institutions, government, and similar settings; the core deliverables of postsecondary political science teachers are courses, learning assessment, and student supervision, with some positions also doing research. The research abilities required overlap, but teaching responsibility and appointment conditions cannot substitute for each other.
entries.question: What is the difference between postsecondary political science teachers and political scientists?

entries.answer: Use the fictional A1–A3 on this page to complete a 45-minute course flow, two discussion questions, a four-dimension rubric, and student feedback. Ask a peer to check with the same rubric whether the mechanism calculation, inference boundary, discussion, and assessment are consistent; observe whether you are willing to keep verifying original texts, chair disagreement, and give feedback on every paper. Interest tests only assist reflection.
entries.question: How do you judge whether postsecondary political science teaching suits you?

entries.answer: There is currently no evidence from which a net reduction of positions in this precise occupation by AI can be inferred. Generative tools can assist with material organization, question variants, and feedback drafts, but fact-checking, teaching judgment, student privacy, academic integrity, and final grading remain with the teacher and institutional rules. The BLS 2025–2035 projection also cannot be attributed to AI.

entries.answer: Evidence is insufficient: the National Bureau of Statistics does not list a separate nationwide occupational median wage for postsecondary political science teachers. The 2025 education industry pre-tax annual average wage was 133,539 yuan/year for urban non-private units and 63,908 yuan/year for private units, only an industry reference across school levels, institutions, and occupations. Individual pay still requires verifying the institution, appointment track, full-time or part-time status, and contract items.

entries.answer: It does not. The 2025 US SOC25-1065 annual median wage is 98,070 dollars, with the 10th and 90th percentiles at 56,450 and 174,660 dollars/year; this takes the O*NET US national row. The statistics cover different institutions and appointment arrangements, and percentiles are not entry-level pay or an academic rank pay grade.

entries.answer: The general US BLS description for postsecondary teachers is that a doctorate is commonly required for four-year colleges and universities, while some positions may accept a master's degree; the specific course, institution, and research tasks change the requirements. In China, verify the hiring institution's announcement, discipline match, teaching and research output, and the higher education teacher qualification process, and a degree must not be equated directly with hiring.

entries.answer: No cross-jurisdictional uniform certificate can be given. The Chinese higher education teacher qualification must be verified through the education authority and the hiring institution's process; obtaining a degree, a training certificate, the teacher qualification, an academic title, and an appointment are different matters. The appointment requirements of specific US institutions also need to be verified position by position.

Using original material, published rubrics, data management under institutional policy, and conflict escalation leaves a reviewable decision record.
